en: The *Jñānāmṛtasāra-saṃhitā* (also known as the *Nārada-pañcarātra*),
the venerable *Nārada-pañcarātra*.
The First Chapter of the First Night. Om, salutation to the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva.
Now, the auspicious invocation.
Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and Nara, the most excellent of men,
as well as to the goddess Sarasvatī, one should then utter the word "Victory."
The gods headed by Gaṇeśa, Śeṣa, Brahmā, and the Sun;
the sages beginning with Kumāra; and the perfected ones (siddhas) such as Kapila and others.
I bow to that one who is higher than the highest, whom Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Durgā, Sāvitrī, Rādhikā, and Parā constantly worship with devotion.
The virtuous ones, as well as the Vaiṣṇava yogins, constantly meditate upon the incomparable,
darkly beautiful form within the light.
One should meditate upon that Supreme Brahman, the Lord who is the Supreme Self—
free from desire, utterly unattached, devoid of qualities, and beyond primordial nature.
The Lord of all, possessing every form, the cause of all causes,
the truth, the eternal, the ancient Puruṣa, supreme and imperishable.
The auspicious one, worthy of auspiciousness, the auspicious itself, the abode of auspiciousness,
consisting of His own will, the supreme abode, the eternal Blessed One.
I praise that Nanda-nandana, who is supreme bliss and full of joy, whom the Vedas eternally extol and whose infinite nature they know.
To Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Rādhikā— the beloved of His devotees, the Master of devotees, whose form is for the grace of devotees, the giver of fortune, the Lord of Fortune, and the abode of Fortune.
Having obtained the nectar of knowledge from the ocean of wisdom, Śaṅkara—
the supreme teacher of the lords of yogis who is both transcendent and immanent— he [attained it].
Having thoroughly churned that ever-new [essence] from the four Vedas—which are like oceans of curd—with the churning-stick of knowledge, [I have extracted this work]. Jss 1.10.10.
Having extracted the fresh butter [of this teaching] and bowed at the lotus feet of Śambhu,
I, Nārada, the son of Brahmā, commence the Pañcarātra.
Oṃ! In the meritorious hermitage of Nārāyaṇa, in the sacred field of Bhārata, at the root of the banyan tree in the Siddha-field of Nārāyaṇa, which bestows great merit.
He was a portion of Kṛṣṇa, a devotee of Kṛṣṇa, a servant of Kṛṣṇa,
and one whose mind was entirely absorbed in meditation upon the lotus feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
The sage Kṛṣṇa-Dvaipāyana was seated comfortably on a pleasant seat, chanting the two syllables "Kṛ-ṣ-ṇ-a," which are the supreme Brahman.
And the sage Śukadeva questioned his omniscient father regarding the cause of the Purāṇas, that which is ancient, supreme, and imperishable.
Śrī Śuka said:
O Blessed One, knower of all principles, who has reached the further shore of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences;
[please explain] whatever kind of knowledge is profound and in accordance with the Śrutis.
Having thoroughly examined all that among them is essential and serves as a lamp for those blinded by ignorance, you should enlighten me. (JSS 1.17)
Now, the praise of devotion to Śrī Kṛṣṇa:
That father is a giver of knowledge who bestows that knowledge which grants devotion to Kṛṣṇa;
and that devotion is supremely pure which bestows service as a servant of Kṛṣṇa. (Jss 1.18)
That alone is praised as true service: the direct attendance upon His feet, eternal residence in Goloka, and the constant chanting of the praises of Hari before Him.
May there be the constant vision of his lotus feet, uninterrupted even by a blink;
may there be the constant engagement in the service of conversation and attendance together with him.
Together with him is the supreme, most beautiful state of uninterruptedness;
it is the desired object for devotees, the very essence as heard in the sacred revelation.
Having heard his son’s words, Vyāsadeva laughed;
recognizing his son as a man of wisdom, he attained supreme joy.
Having bestowed auspicious blessings upon his son, the All-Knowing One, the Embodiment of All Realization,
began to speak that which he had received from the mouth of his Guru.
Śrī Vyāsa said:
O Śuka, you are blessed, you are venerable, and you are of meritorious form in this land of Bhārata;
by you, our son, our lineage has been liberated and purified.
That son is a devotee of Kṛṣṇa who brings great fame in Bhārata;
by his mere birth, he effortlessly purifies a hundred lineages of men. (Jss 1.25)
One hundred [generations] of maternal grandfathers, the mother, the mother’s mother,
as well as uterine siblings, kinsmen, servants, and the wife together with one's own children.
The one who accepts the maiden, the three preceding male ancestors,
the giver of the maiden, and the father-in-law— all these, together with their wives, are liberated while still alive.
The Lord himself was the creator, supremely devoted to Kṛṣṇa;
Vasiṣṭha, his son, was himself a devotee of Kṛṣṇa and a Vaiṣṇava.
His son was Śakti, a Vaiṣṇava whose mind was solely intent on meditation upon Kṛṣṇa;
and his son was Parāśara, who [attained perfection] through service to the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa.
I am liberated while living, a possessor of great knowledge, the teacher of the teachers of the lords of yogis, and I am divided by the Vedas through service at the feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. Jss 1.1.30.
The venerable sage Nārada, the lord of yogis, is my direct guru;
and Śambhu, the guru of the gurus of the lords of yogis, is my guru’s guru.
By their merit you have become their son, a personified mass of merit;
you are the light of the lotuses, of me, and of men—you are the Sun himself.
Having offered salutations to the lotus feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, to the lotus feet of Nārada and Vyāsa,
and to Sarasvatī, I shall declare the eternal knowledge.
Listen to the *Pañcarātra*, the desired essence of the Vedas,
which is esteemed as the fivefold dialogue and longed for by devotees.
The supreme, pure, auspicious nectar of knowledge, dearer than life itself.
Now, what are the six dialogues?
Indeed, in Goloka and on the mountain Śataśṛṅga.
On the most auspicious bank of the Virajā, at the charming foot of a banyan tree,
and before Rādhikā, [he saw] Brahmā, who was born from a lotus.
Having heard this meritorious Pañcarātra, the Ordainer of the worlds spoke to his son, that great devotee who was praising him and bowing before him.
Having bowed down to Rādhikā and Kṛṣṇa, he went to the temple of Śiva;
there, Śaṅkara worshipped him with devotion and the highest respect.
To him who was seated comfortably on a pleasant seat, composed, devoted, and honored,
the humble one respectfully inquired after his well-being in a manner that brought him joy.
He related all of that auspicious [teaching], beginning with the *Pañcarātra*,
concerning his dwelling at the foot of the banyan tree and on the banks of the Mandākinī in heaven.
Having spoken that nectar of knowledge concerning the Lord praised by the lords of yogins, the lords of siddhas, and the lords of sages, he departed for the world of Brahmā.
And Śambhu spoke it to his own disciple, the sage Nārada;
Nārada, in turn, recounted it at Puṣkara during the solar eclipse festival.
To me, your devoted and affectionate follower, on this auspicious day in the assembly of sages,
[I shall teach] this pure Pañcarātra, which is a lamp for destroying the blindness of delusion.
Now, the explanation of the term *pañcarātra*: "Night" (*rātra*) is a word for knowledge (*jñāna*), and knowledge is said to be fivefold;
therefore, the wise proclaim this as *pañcarātra*.
Knowledge is the supreme reality and the remover of birth, death, and old age;
therefore, Śambhu obtained Mṛtyuñjaya from the mouth of Kṛṣṇa.
This second knowledge is supreme and desired by those seeking liberation;
it is pure and bestows ultimate release, for through it one is absorbed in the state of Hari.
The third is pure knowledge, which bestows devotion to Kṛṣṇa and the requested service to Him, through which one obtains the servitude of Lord Hari. (Jss 1.47)

The fourth is the technical knowledge (*yaugika-jñāna*), which is supreme and bestows all accomplishments; it is the very essence of all yogins, my son, and the giver of bliss to the perfected ones (*siddhas*). (JSS 1.48)
Atomicity, lightness, pervasiveness, irresistible will, greatness,
as well as lordship, mastery, and likewise the power of determining objects at will.
The contemptuous [power], hearing from afar, entering another's body, the multiplication of bodies, the gift of life, and the supreme taking of another's life. Jss 1.50.
The art of being the creator of emanation, the cause of emanation and withdrawal, and the sixteenfold perfection from which it arises for the wise; Jss_1,1.51 //
And that which is declared to be the supreme knowledge for men is indeed the worldly [knowledge];
for Māyā, who is the beloved goddess, is the cause of ultimate delusion.
The mind bound to sense objects, the indulgence of all the senses, and the constant nurturing of one's own family and oneself—[these are the ways of the world]. (Jss 1.53)
The first is sattvic knowledge, the second is that very same [knowledge],
and the third is the knowledge of being beyond the qualities (nirguṇya), which is supreme in every respect.
The wise man does not desire that fourth [type of] food which is rajasic, nor does he desire that fifth knowledge which is tamasic.
The wise know that the Pañcarātra is declared to be fivefold in knowledge;
yet the Pañcarātra is also sevenfold, the supreme bestower of knowledge upon the wise.
The Brāhma, Śaiva, Kaumāra, Vāsiṣṭha, Kāpila, Gautamīya, and Nāradīya—this is remembered as the sevenfold [tradition]. (Jss 1.57)
Now, the praise of the texts:
The Pañcarātra, the Vedas, and the Purāṇas in their entirety;
the Itihāsa, the Dharmaśāstra, and the Śāstra born of Siddhiyoga.
Having seen and surveyed everything, and having obtained knowledge from Śaṅkara,
the sage Nārada composed the *Jñānāmṛta-pañcarātra*.
O son, it is merit that obstructs sin, bestows devotion and service to Hari,
is the very essence of all Vaiṣṇavas, dear to them, and more precious than life itself.
The Nārada-pancaratra, which is the very essence of all the Vedas and most wonderful, is extremely difficult to find even among the Purāṇas.
The Blessed One is the inner self of all, the eternal light of Brahman,
the most perfect and glorious one, just as Kṛṣṇa is among the gods.
Just as she is the worshipful Mūlaprakṛti and Īśvarī among the goddesses,
so too is Śiva [the worshipful one] among Vaiṣṇavas, Siddhas, the wise, and yogins.
Brahmā is the lord of the senses when they are trusting, of the mind which moves swiftly, of those who know the Vedas, and of those worthy of worship; so too is Gaṇeśvara.
Just as the venerable Sanatkumāra is the foremost among sages, as Bṛhaspati is among the intelligent, and as Kapila is among the perfected ones (siddhas); Jss_1.1.65.
Among the masters of yoga he is the pure sage Nārāyaṇa;
among poets he is like Śukra, and among scholars he is like Bṛhaspati.
Just as the Gaṅgā is among rivers, the ocean of waters among seas, Vṛndāvana among forests, and Bhārata among the lands; Jss_1,1.67 //
Among sacred fords, Puṣkara is like the Vaiṣṇava among those worthy of worship;
it is like the ether of the self among attainments, and like the city of Kāśī among cities.
Among trees, he is the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa); among cows, the fragrant Kāmadhenu;
among flowers, the Pārijāta; and among leaves, Tulasī.
Among mantras, the Kṛṣṇa-mantra is supreme; among sciences, it is like the best; among riches, it is likewise the foremost;
as the sun is among luminous bodies, so is it the nectar among sweet things.
O son, just as Mahāviṣṇu is the support of all gross things, so too is the atom the support of all subtle things; and he who bestows the mantras and tantras is the support of all that is heavy.
And a son is the foremost among those objects of affection, as the moon is among the stars,
as clarified butter is among products of the cow, and as the desired grain is among cultivated crops.
As the Vedas are among the scriptures, as the twice-born is among those in the stages of life, and as the pearl, ruby, and diamond are among luminous gems; 1.73.
Just as Gāyatrī is among the meters in the Veda, Durgā among the powerful goddesses,
Lakṣmī among those devoted to their husbands, and Medinī among those of a forgiving nature.
Among fortunate and beautiful women, and among those dear to Kṛṣṇa,
she is supreme, just as Hanumān is among monkeys and Garuḍa among birds.
Among powerful mounts, it is like the bull of Śaṅkara;
among ritual objects, the Śālagrāma is supreme; and among all forms of worship, the worship of Kṛṣṇa is the highest.
O son, among vows the Ekādaśī is foremost; among austerities, fasting is like unto it; among sacrifices, the sacrifice of recitation (japa-yajña) is supreme; and among duties, truth is the highest.
Good character is [the representative of] virtues; the chanting of Kṛṣṇa’s glories is [the representative of] meritorious deeds;
splendor is [the representative of] things beautiful and pleasant to behold; and radiance is [the representative of] brilliance in every respect.
Just as a mother is the benefactor and friend of her nursing children,
so too is Śeṣa, the lord of the worlds, honored among the nāgas in this world.
Sudarśana among weapons and Viśvakarman among artisans [were born] among the great divine sages who were most righteous and compassionate.
Just as the sage Nārada is honored among the wise devotees of Viṣṇu,
so too is the Pañcarātra honored among all the scriptures.
Just as one who has drunk the nectar of immortality has no longing for other things,
so the virtuous, having mastered the *Pañcarātra*, have no longing for anything else.
It is the seed of the knowledge of all things, a lamp for those blinded by ignorance, the essence extracted from the Vedas, and the reality desired by all. (JSS 1.83)
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "Praise of the Text," in the First Night of the glorious Nārada-Pañcarātra. Śuka said:
The Second Chapter of the First Night.
Śuka said:
Or where, O dear one, was the Pañcarātra bestowed upon the wise Nārada by Śambhu? You should explain that to me.
Now follows the description of Nārada’s asceticism.
Vyāsa said:
Having studied all the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas in the presence of his father, [he departed].
He went to Kedāra, which is highly praised in the land of Bhārata.
To the east of the Himalayas, on the enchanting bank of the Gaṅgā,
lies the Siddha Nārāyaṇa-kṣetra, desired by all.
That sage performed divine austerity for a thousand years,
remaining constantly pure and strictly adhering to the very method prescribed by his father.
At the conclusion of his ascetic penance, the great sage heard a voice from the sky—
a voice consisting of few syllables yet rich in meaning, which brought happiness in its ultimate result.
Then an incorporeal divine voice spoke to Nārada:
"If Hari has been secured by your ascetic penance, then what need is there for more?"
If Hari is not held within, what is the use of austerity?
If Hari is both within and without, what is the use of austerity?
If Hari is neither within nor without, what is the use of austerity?
Desist, desist, O Brahmin! Why these austerities, my child?
Go, go quickly, O twice-born one, to Śaṅkara, the ocean of knowledge! Attain, attain the fully matured devotion to Hari as taught by the Vaiṣṇavas!
And it is the shears that cut the bonds of the shackles of existence.
Having heard this, that sage became despondent; on the bank of the celestial river, he reflected upon the meaning [of what he had heard], yet his mind found no peace.
Weeping on the bank of the celestial river while repeatedly remembering the feet of Hari,
he beheld before him his father Brahmā together with Kumāra.
He suddenly bowed his head to his father and his uterine brother;
the sage quickly and respectfully offered them water for their feet and the guest-offering.
He questioned the Youth, the Ordainer of the worlds, who was seated comfortably, very steady, smiling, and free from fatigue, regarding the meaning of the two verses.

With eyes full of tears and his body covered in horripilation, he bowed with devotion, his neck bent low, before him who delights in his own self, whose desires are fulfilled, who is the teacher of the teachers of the wise.
Having heard Nārada’s words and seeing him so distressed,
Brahmā consulted with his son and began to provide an explanation.
Then, for the sake of explaining the meaning of the divine speech, Brahmā said:
"O child, the meaning of the previous verse is profound and is in accord with the Vedas."
The Vaidikas provide a twofold, pure exposition of the meaning of the Vedas.
O Nārada, if Hari has been propitiated by a person through his own devotion, what is the use of fruitless asceticism for one who is already purified by sacred fords?
In India, the asceticism of one who is liberated while living and a devotee of the Kṛṣṇa-mantra is a seed for ridicule as well as mere re-chewing of what has already been chewed. (Jss 1.2.16)
O son, by the mere utterance of the mantra, it effortlessly purifies a hundred men, each with their respective devotees and kinsmen. (Jss 1.2.17)
There is no dharma and no austerity higher than service to Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
indeed, for a Vaiṣṇava, austerity is merely fruitless labor.
O son, for one who worships the mantra of Kṛṣṇa and is purified by sacred fords,
bathing at holy sites and fasting are mere mockery according to the Vedas.
Whatever sin a Vaiṣṇava may have committed in accordance with past karma is destroyed by the mere reception of the mantra, just as grass is consumed by fire.
The supreme fire is pure, and water is pure and stainless;
the land of Bhārata is pure, as is the sacred site that is a leaf of tulasī.
One who is pure and devoted to Kṛṣṇa purifies these [worlds] with ease;
even these [deities] long for the mere touch of such a devotee with great respect.
The earth is instantly purified by the dust of the devotee's feet;
indeed, there is no one in the three worlds more pure than a servant of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
That man who performs the worship of Kṛṣṇa upon the discus-marked Śāligrāma stone,
and who daily partakes of its water for the feet and its food offerings, [attains the supreme goal].
That Vaiṣṇava, greatly purified and devoted to his mantra, being pure,
sanctifies a hundred men along with their kinsmen merely by birth.
"Child, one quarter of the verse has been explained according to the tradition;
listen as I explain the other quarter according to my own understanding. (Jss 1.26)
If Hari has not been propitiated by that lowest of men, what is the use of his asceticism? That labor is vain and fruitless.
For indeed, vows, gifts, austerities, fasts,
the study of the Vedas, sacrifices,
and auspicious ritual acts do not purify one who lacks devotion, just as a river cannot purify a jar of liquor.
By the mere touch of the non-devotee, the sacred fords trembled;
by the burden of the non-devotee, that Earth herself was shaken.
"O child, half a verse has been spoken according to the tradition; listen as I provide the explanation of even that half-verse. Jss 1.2.30.
The essence of the Vedas is the doctrine of Kṛṣṇa; this is not my own fabrication, for it belongs to those great-souled men who perceive [the truth] both internally and externally.
O Sage, for them, asceticism practiced constantly whether in sleep or wakefulness is fruitless;
yet that very person, who is equal to Viṣṇu, is indeed a portion of Him in the land of Bhārata.
By means of the binding of protection for that [mantra], Sudarśana,
through mere meditation upon it, becomes free from sin and purifies the three worlds.
Having given the discus for the sake of protection, Janārdana is not free from anxiety;
he himself goes near it to see it and to ensure its guarding.
Indeed, there is no one dearer to Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul, than one who is devoted to Him;
for neither the self, nor the vital breaths, nor the limbs and so forth,
nor Lakṣmī, Rādhikā, Vāṇī, Brahmā, or even Śambhu himself, is dearer than a devotee.
For Kṛṣṇa has his life-force in his devotees, and the Vaiṣṇavas indeed have their life-force in Kṛṣṇa;
the Vaiṣṇavas meditate upon Kṛṣṇa, and Kṛṣṇa likewise [meditates] upon the Vaiṣṇavas.
O Lord of Sages, you have explained three quarters [of this work] according to the scriptures;
now listen as I provide the explanation of the remaining quarter.
O Nārada, if Hari is neither within nor without for those men whose hearts are inwardly defiled, their asceticism is likewise in vain.
Of what use is that knowledge, austerity, vow, or restraint,
or even pilgrimage to sacred fords and merit, for those whose minds are deluded by a lack of devotion?
A dog-cooker (outcaste) is greater than twice-born men who are devoid of devotion to Kṛṣṇa;
even a multitude of barbarians is superior by virtue of practicing their own duty.
Brahmins who have fallen away from their own dharma, as well as those who eat forbidden food and constantly practice unrighteousness, become outcasts, the lowest of dog-cookers.
And the specific duty of the brāhmaṇas is the constant service of Kṛṣṇa;
those virtuous ones eternally partake of His food offerings and the water from His feet.
If that lowest of the twice-born eats without having first offered food to Hari,
the wise know his food to be equal to excrement and his water to be equal to urine.
The boar and the barbarian, as well as the lowest of outcastes, eat their own proper food;
but the Brahmin who constantly eats what is unfit to be eaten falls from his status.
And one verse has been explained; now, O Nārada, understand as it is the knowledge of the other half, and its explanation as is appropriate. (Jss 1.2.45)
"O Brahmin, desist from asceticism; the asceticism of a devotee is certainly fruitless.
By making Śaṅkara your guru, you shall soon attain devotion to Hari."
Well-matured devotion to Hari is the boat for crossing over the ocean of worldly existence;
the Guru alone is the Supreme Brahman, appearing in the form of a helmsman.
Having spoken thus, the goddess Sarasvatī departed;
her intention has been explained. What more shall I tell you?
And having heard the words of Brahmā, the blessed Sanat-kumāra, the teacher of yogins, laughed and spoke to his father, O Śuka.
Sanatkumāra said: "The explanation of the previous verse was not understood by me, who am but a child;
it is proper to enlighten again a son, a disciple, and one who is ignorant."
If the penance of one by whom Hari has been propitiated is in vain, and if the penance of one by whom Hari has not been propitiated is also in vain; Jss_1,2.51 //
How is it that those two are devoid of that [dharma], and how can there be a place for austerity?
O dear one, explain this to me, a child, as I practice austerity. Jss 1.2.52.
Having heard his son’s words, the teacher of the worlds became doubtful;
O Śuka, he meditated upon the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa, the supreme wish-fulfilling tree.
Having reflected for a moment upon his lotus feet, he attained his desired conclusion;
even the Creator of the worlds then began to provide the exposition.
Now, the praise of the food offering (naivedya):
Brahmā said:
"I am blessed by you, the son of the Guru of gurus and the teacher of the wise."
A father is happy through a son who is devoted to Viṣṇu, most virtuous, and a true son.
"You are blessed, you are wise, and you are a devotee of Hari, my son;
O learned one, through you both my birth and my life have become fruitful."
Understand the meaning of the preceding verse; I shall provide an explanation once more.
Even so, if you are not satisfied, you shall provide the explanation yourself.
The prefix *sam-* signifies "perfectly," and the root *rādh* denotes "attainment.
Thus, he by whom Hari has been perfectly attained (*saṃprāpta*)—for him, the labor of asceticism is rendered fruitless. (JSS 1.2.58)
In whatever manner Hari, the Lord, was truly attained—
whether known in a dream or in waking knowledge— the labor of their asceticism was rendered fruitless.
Neither pilgrimage, charity, austerity, merit, nor vows can ever purify that most base of men— a fool who is averse to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, even if he be a twice-born brahmin.
He who is the most deluded in the world and he who has attained supreme devotion—both of these succeed easily; it is the middling ones who practice asceticism.
The middling person worships other gods as well, knows Hari and is intent upon Him, and performs austerities, desiring to attain Him. (JSS 1.2.62)
And a householder who is devoted from former times, though bound by worldly existence, performs the desired austerity for the sake of the lotus feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (JSS 1.2.63)
Supreme is the worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, meditation upon Him, the chanting of His names, and the eating of the water from His feet and the food offerings; this fulfills every desire. (JSS 1.2.64)
And the brahmin was exceedingly deluded due to the fault of his previous guru;
for being of a tamasic nature, he did not know Śrī Kṛṣṇa to be beyond the three modes of material nature.
Whether through ignorance or knowledge, by virtue of past association with the virtuous,
one partakes of the food offering (naivedya) of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord.
And he shall be liberated, my son; he is released from all sins.
He goes by means of a divine vehicle to Goloka, the supreme world.
Listen, my child, I shall relate an ancient narrative from of old,
which is exceedingly pleasant to hear, beautiful, sweet, and supreme in bestowing liberation.
Kānyakubja, Sukṣubdha, the Brāhmaṇa village-priest,
Devala, Vṛṣavāha, Mahāmūḍha, and Pātakin.
In dream-consciousness, one does not recognize merit, nor the worship of Kṛṣṇa, nor the auspicious conversation, sight, or touch of a devotee of Kṛṣṇa. (Jss 1.2.70)
For a mere moment, that which was previously very difficult for him to obtain became possible;
by that merit, the brahmin received an offering of food (naivedya) for Kṛṣṇa.
Through the merit of his father, the son [obtained] that which had fallen on the path,
as well as what remained after he himself had eaten, which had fallen from a Vaiṣṇava.
And as that brahmin was walking there, a very oily, aged, and highly refined food item mixed with dust fell down.
O son, while Kṛṣṇa was in a hurry over the food offering, that substance mixed with Kṛṣṇa’s *naivedya* was eaten by the brāhmaṇa. (Jss 1.2.74)
Afflicted by hunger along with his son, the two went home;
and the husband-devoted wife ate the remnants of the brahmin's meal.
Through that continuous succession, she became truly purified;
and that Brahmin, together with his son, became one liberated while living.
By that merit earned at that time, O twice-born one, she who had been eaten by a tiger in the forest went to Goloka together with the two sons of the tiger;
for she, being devoted to her husband, had died along with her lord and thus went with him.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Praise of Naivedya," in the *Jñānāmṛtasāra* of the *Śrī-Nārada-Pañcarātra*, within the dialogue between Brahmā and Sanatkumāra during the first *ekarātra*.

yet they wander perpetually in the realm of sense-objects, deluded by the Māyā of Hari.
I am neither the protector, nor the creator, nor the destroyer of living beings;
I am detached, an ascetic, and intent upon the worship of Hari.
In the past, Śrī Kṛṣṇa gave me the domain of dissolution;
having given that to Rudra, I am now devoted to the ascetic penances of Hari.
By means of worshipping him, by meditation, by austerity, and by adoration;
by means of hymns, by armor-rites, and indeed by the recitation of the name-mantras.
I am the conqueror of death; now I have no fear of time.
Time destroys everything, except for me and likewise the Lord.
In the past, at the first creation of all things, there were certain Rudras born from the forehead of a creator; among them, I am one, Śaṅkara.
And at the dissolution of Brahmā’s kalpa, during both the elemental and the natural destructions,
all those attached to sense objects perish, but not so the devotees who are like the Lord himself.
The passing of incalculable Brahmās and likewise incalculable eons has already occurred;
how many kinds [of them] will there be again and again?
In a single blink of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s eye, Brahmā may fall;
therein, all material beings disappear again and again.
I am neither an ordinary being nor a seeker of sense objects; I am a Vaiṣṇava with an eternal body.
By the boon of Hari, I am immortal, and therefore I am the support of Śiva.
And at the time of elemental dissolution, the entire flood of the universe, from the realm of Brahmā downwards, is certainly submerged in water, with the sole exception of the supreme abode of Kṛṣṇa.
All the goddesses have dissolved, and Kṛṣṇa is truly and most certainly [the reality];
all male beings have dissolved into the eternal and primordial Truth.
I and Kṛṣṇa are the Prakṛti and the foremost attendant of Hari;
we are eternally present in the ever-abiding and flawless Goloka.
"From the very beginning of creation until the end, there is but one Lord, not a second;
for His devotees do not perish even during the dissolution of both primordial nature (prakṛti) and its evolutes (prākṛta)."
Through constant remembrance of him and of his supreme devotees, there shall be no depletion of one's lifespan; how then could death occur?
No inauspiciousness exists anywhere for the devotees of Vāsudeva;
and by the constant remembrance of those supreme devotees, [all evil is destroyed].
In this kalpa, no fear of birth, death, old age, or disease shall arise; you, O Brahmā, shall be the establisher of duties therein.
"And O Creator, provide a place for these fires of wrath; perform whatever rite is necessary.
Having heard Śambhu’s words, the lotus-seated Brahmā trembled and, by the command of Śaṅkara, prepared a site for the fires.
Brahmā said:
Fever has three feet, three heads, six arms, and nine eyes;
he is fierce, with ashes as his weapon, resembling Yama, the Ender of Time at the dissolution of the world.
Let the fire of the wrath of existence now prevail everywhere;
I have already performed my duty toward these common bodies.
O Śambhu, let the fire of my wrath become the consecrated fire of a twice-born;
I have ordained that its function shall prevail everywhere.
O Śiva, let the fire of the wrath of Śeṣa now reside within the mouth of Śeṣa,
so that at the time of universal dissolution he may consume the entire world like a lump of cow dung.
Among fires, the primary fire is Viśva; the fire of worldly transaction is Īśvara.
Indeed, let it be everywhere the benefactor of all.
May this fire of the wrath of Dharmāsya and this black fire (kṛṣṇāgni) arise;
it shall perform the complete incineration of all those who practice unrighteousness.
This is the fire of the sun's wrath and the forest fire in the woods;
its abode is upon the trunk of this tree, and its prey consists of beasts and birds.
The fire of the moon’s wrath, which is the fire of separation for lovers throughout the world,
constantly consumes the bodies of both husband and wife when they are parted.
The fire of Indra’s wrath immediately became the thunderbolt-fire,
and the fire of Upendra likewise became this lightning.
May this fire of the Rudras, the fire of the great meteor,
become the fire of Gaṇeśa, remaining in its proper place upon the earth.
Wherever it might remain, that very place becomes saline; thus do the wise know it.
And indeed, the fire of Skanda’s wrath became the fire of the weapon in battle.
There, the sage Aurva, the son of Brahmā, took into himself the fire from the mouths of the gods who were other than those of desire and from the mouths of the sages.
Having placed his right thigh [upon the seat] according to the Vedic mantras,
and having paid homage to Brahmā and Śaṅkara, that sage departed for asceticism.
Therefore, O son, having emerged from that at the proper time, he himself became in ancient times the Vāḍava fire in the ocean, known as the Aurva fire.
Seeing the fierce fire of desire, Brahmā reflected in his mind and deliberated together with the gods and the lords of sages in an assembly.
He summoned all the women who were virtuous and devoted to their husbands;
all those ladies approached and spoke to the Lotus-born One.
The women said:
"O Blessed One, tell us what; instruct us, what shall we do?
Having reflected upon everything with your mind, lay the burden upon us, for we are women."
Brahmā said:
"Having taken up the fire of desire that bestows pleasure in sexual union,
may all women in the universe be eternally possessed of longing."
Having heard the words of Brahmā, all those women, casting aside their fear in that assembly, spoke to him with eyes and faces reddened by anger.
The women said:
"Fie on you! The Supreme Lord has rendered the Creator of the world useless;
he is no longer worthy of worship due to the curse of Mohinī and now, by the curse of his own son."
Having grasped the fire of passion, both men and women constantly and perpetually burn with a supreme, unbearable, and truly real [suffering].
A single part of that resides in a man, and three parts reside in a woman;
therefore, all women have been milked by us—what need have we for others?
If you surrender yourself to a man because of the fire of passion that burns within us, we shall reduce you to ashes; who then will be your protector?
Having heard the words of the devoted wife, Śiva himself spoke to her that which was beneficial, true, the essence of ethics, and bringing happiness in the end.
Now, regarding the origin of the unchaste woman,
the illustrious Mahādeva said: "O noble one, abandon now the duality [of passion] along with those of virtuous vows."
And the splendor of those devoted to their husbands shall be superior to all others.
O Lord of Gods, O Sovereign, create a magical being of the female kind;
bestow upon her the supreme seed of suffering: the fire of lust and anger.
Having heard the words of Śaṅkara, the Creator of the worlds quickly fashioned at that very moment a form in the shape of a woman, most enchanting to the mind.
"Oh, what beauty! Oh, what attire! Oh, her fresh youth!
Oh, her eyes and sidelong glances, which bewilder even the minds of sages! (Jss 1.14.56)
Oh, how firm and beautiful is this pair of breasts, so well-rounded! And how wonderful is this pair of hips—so variegated, firm, and full! Jss 1.14.57
Her pair of hips are rounded, wheel-shaped, and very delicate;
they possess the hue of the white campaka flower, and every limb is desirable.
His face is exceedingly beautiful, surpassing ten million full moons of autumn;
with a joyful countenance and a slight smile, it is delightedly covered with a cloth.
His body is very delicate, moving, neither too tall nor too short,
always clothed in garments purified by fire and adorned with jewel ornaments.
Shaped like a pomegranate or a water lily, dense and beautiful with vermilion,
together with a drop of musk and smooth drops of sandalwood paste.
The upper lip is like the shape of a ripe bimba fruit,
and the two rows of teeth are like the seeds of a pomegranate.
Beholding her, whose beautiful mass of braided hair was adorned with garlands of jasmine,
the Lotus-born One kindled the fire of desire within her.
Seeing his moon-like form, she became intoxicated with desire and lost her composure;
casting a sidelong glance with a smiling face, she said to me, "Devote yourself to me."
Overwhelmed with shame, Candra departed from the floor of the assembly;
and she, afflicted by desire and having lost her modesty, beheld Kāma and desired him.
Kāma fled from him, and she ran after him;
all the deities and the sages also laughed in the assembly.
All the women were ashamed and unable to restrain her;
Śaṅkara and all the others mocked the group of women.
Not having obtained her desire, that woman returned and,
in the assembly and in the presence of the gods, spoke to that Aśvinī-kumāra:
The Kṛtyā-Kāminī said:
"O son of the Sun, joyfully accept me, your beloved Rasavatī—
me who grant pleasure in the erotic sentiment, who am peaceful, supreme, overcome by desire, and excellent."
I shall wander with you in the beautiful, dense forest;
in secret and secluded places, I shall sport with you day and night.
I shall provide honey-wine, fragrant and pure water,
betel-leaf with camphor, and delightful articles of enjoyment.
Having prepared a delightful bed, honored with flowers and sandalwood,
I shall anoint the Blessed One with flowers and sandalwood paste.
The prince said:
"O lovely one, cast aside deceit— which destroys righteousness— and speak words to me that are pleasing to my heart, O charming woman."
What is the duty of women, what is their mental inclination, and what is their inherent nature? Of how many kinds is their conduct? You should explain that to me. (Jss 1,14.74)
Having heard the words of the son of Aśvinī, she, afflicted by desire, said to him:
"Where is there shame for those tormented by passion, and where is fear or even pride? (Jss 1.14.75)
Now, regarding the description of the nature of an unchaste woman,
the passionate woman said:
"There is no place, there is no moment, and there is no excellent messenger."
By that very means, the virtue of chastity arises in young women.
Seeing her lover well-dressed, the passionate woman, afflicted by desire,
experiences a night of horripilation and intense itching in her womb.
And she would become senseless, tormented by the fever of passion;
for that reason, she abandons everything—son, beloved, home, and wealth.
Having obtained a young man, she abandons her native land;
yet, having obtained one even superior to him, she would abandon that very person in an instant.
Having obtained a young Mleccha husband, the best among the virtuous, she was capable of administering poison to her lord, yet she was eager to give him her all.
One should abandon fear of one's family, shame, dharma, kin, fame,
and fortune upon encountering a youth who is a hero in pleasure and intent on sexual union.
Whose mind can one know—that which possesses a most pleasing and beautiful face, speech that is ever sweet, yet a heart like the edge of a razor? Jss 1,14.82
Just as a flash of lightning in water or a streak in the sky is unstable,
so too is the affection of an unchaste woman unstable, as are her words, which are like a dream.
For unchaste women, there is neither truth nor righteousness, neither fear nor compassion;
they possess neither worldly decorum nor shame, being constantly preoccupied with their paramours.
Whether in dreams or while awake, whether eating or lying down, she is always constantly preoccupied with thoughts of desire; her affection is for her lover alone and for no one else.
Unchaste women, wicked-minded and merciless, are more dangerous than those who kill men; for the sake of a lover, they even kill their own son—what need is there to mention their other relatives?
For even the Vedas do not know that which is so deeply rooted in the heart;
how then could the gods, the sages, and the virtuous know this certainty?
Upon seeing a beloved who is a hero in pleasure, one should treat him like milk or ghee;
but when his youth has passed and he is seen to be withered, one should abandon him in an instant, as if seeing poison.
Therefore, the virtuous should never place their trust in that wicked woman;
for there is no enemy on earth for men greater than a corrupt woman.
Poison is certainly neutralized by a mantra, fire by water,
a thorn by being extracted with fire, and a wicked person is brought under control by praise.
A greedy man is brought under control by wealth, and a king is always submissive to service;
an enemy is subdued by a mixture of one's own pure nature and the threat of fear.
A learned brahmin is won over by respect; a youth by the weight of love;
a kinsman by impartiality; and a teacher always by prostrations.
A fool is under the sway of a story, and a learned man is under the sway of the investigation of knowledge;
for a wicked unchaste woman does not come under the control of a man.
Love, when directed toward its own proper object, should always be constant and in accordance with duty;
it does not come under the control of everyone except through intense passion (*śṛṅgāra*).
Neither by affection, nor by wealth, nor by praise, nor by service,
nor even by the gift of one's life, can a courtesan be brought under control for even a moment.
Their food is twofold, their intelligence fourfold,
their counsel sixfold, and their passion is said to be eightfold.
A woman of loose character who constantly indulges her desires is never satiated by her play;
she increases all the more, like a fire fed with clarified butter.
If that man indulges in amorous dalliance day and night, there is still no satisfaction for unchaste women; they desire to devour the man.
Fire is never satiated with wood, nor is the great ocean with rivers;
Death is never satiated with all living beings, nor is he ever satiated with these riches.
The minds of the virtuous are never satiated with excellence, just as the submarine fire is never satiated with waters,
nor the earth with dust, nor a unchaste woman with men.
Thus, only a little has been told; it is not appropriate to speak of everything.
Know, O son of the Sun, that modesty is the seed of women.
And having heard the words of the female Kṛtyā, O son, the sages and the gods laughed,
while all the women, including Padmā and the others, were overcome with shame and remained silent.
With her face bowed in modesty, Lakṣmī emerged from the circle of gods;
following after her, Pārvatī likewise emerged with Sarasvatī, her face bowed low.
Sāvitrī, Rohiṇī, Svāhā, Vāruṇī, Rati, and Śacī—
all came together in one place and held a consultation.
Having summoned the sorceress-women, they spoke to them in turn;
those women then obstructed that beloved woman, even though she was well-guarded.
Suśīlā, whose abode was the lotus, placed her hand upon her face and bestowed this auspicious blessing: "May you be modest, O daughter; may you be peaceful."
Sarasvatī bestowed upon her self-conceit, fortitude, loquacity, eloquence, counsel, and self-protection.
And Sāvitrī bestowed upon her excellent character, which is exceedingly difficult to find,
as well as self-concealment, profundity, and the fear of [losing] family honor.
Pārvatī said:
"Fie on you, you naturally unchaste woman! Be ashamed, O beautiful one;
preserve your self-respect and dignity, for we are afflicted by love."
Having manifested a bodily array throughout the entire earth,
may you obtain each of the eightfold human desires individually.
Possessing fourfold modesty and likewise twofold fortitude, go toward the virtue of the desire for non-enjoyment; go far away from my presence!
The desire of men is twofold compared to that of actual women;
their modesty is eightfold, and their fortitude is fourfold.
By my command, let family dharma, family fear, virtuous conduct, and exalted pride abide forever in men and in women alike.
Because he was devoid of shame before everyone in the assembly, that lowest of gods asked about the nature of women; therefore, he shall not partake in the sacrifice.
From this day forward, by my command, that which is joined with impurity shall not be accepted from anyone, nor shall it be eaten by physicians or learned men.
Having spoken thus, the goddesses and all the women departed,
as did the gods, the sages, and whoever else had assembled there.
O son, even among the gods, the sages, and all others everywhere,
modesty is the very seed of women who are devoted to their husbands.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Origin of the Kulaṭā," in the first *ekarātra* of the *Jñānāmṛtasāra*, within the illustrious *Nārada-pañcarātra*.
[Now begins] the fifteenth chapter of the first *ekarātra*.
When the appointed time had passed, the Gandharva Upavarhaṇa,
by means of his own yogic power, abandoned his body in Bhārata, for alas, he was hindered by his former [karmic] state.
He was born from a Śūdra womb due to his father’s curse and the power of destiny;
yet, having received the grace of Viṣṇu, he became the son of Brahmā.
Released from his father’s curse and having attained supreme knowledge,
he possessed the recollection of his past lives through the grace of Kṛṣṇa’s mantra.
Having come from his father, he received the incomparable Śrī-Kṛṣṇa mantra from Candraśekhara on the banks of the celestial Gaṅgā.
Accompanied by his preceptor Śaṅkara, he departed swiftly from the banks of the celestial Gaṅgā to the presence of Pārvatī.
Śambhu and the great sage Nārada dwelt there,
as did Pārvatī, Bhadrakālī, Skanda, and Gaṇapati himself.
Mahākāla, Nandin, and the powerful Vīrabhadra;
the Siddhas, the great seers, and the sages such as Saṅka and others.
All the lords of yogis and the wise spoke in the assembly of Śambhu regarding the hymn,
the armor-verse, and the meditation for Subhadrā in the forest.
In ancient times, the venerable sage Nārāyaṇa imparted to a brahmin the procedure for worship, including all that precedes it with the preparatory rites (puraścaraṇa).
The Blessed Śambhu gave that very [teaching] to Nārada;
and there, in the presence of Pārvatī, the celestial sage, the great muni Nārada, spoke to Śambhu, the teacher of teachers of yogins.
O Blessed One, knower of all phenomena, omniscient one, cause of all things:
you ought to explain to me that which was previously asked by me.
O Brahmin, whatever has been asked by you, both individually and in sequence, ask further, O Sage; let the members of my assembly listen.
And that which is internal knowledge—the supreme essence of the Vedas, the essence among those who possess knowledge, the auspicious bestower of devotion to Kṛṣṇa. (Jss 1.15.13)
Knowledge that bestows liberation and nirvāṇa cuts through the very root of karma;
through the yoga of its accomplishment, liberation is indeed the desired goal even for yogins.
Knowledge concerning the objects of cyclic existence is perpetually enveloped in delusion;
[so too is] the conduct of the stages of life, which is adorned by their respective dharmas.
O Maheśvara, [this applies] to the four castes and the four stages of life,
to the mendicants, the Vaiṣṇavas, the ascetics, and the celibate students.
And likewise for those in the stage of forest-dwellers (vānaprastha), for the learned,
and for women devoted to their husbands— whatever [merit] there is, as well as whatever worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa there may be.

Whatever hymn, armor-mantra, or desired preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is intended for all daily observances, as well as the fruition of the actions of those who live by their work; [may that be accomplished].
The characteristics of Prakṛti and Īśvara are bound by the latent impressions (vāsanā) of saṃsāra;
or rather, it is the description of the descent of that Brahman which is beyond those two.
Who is that which has descended as a fraction (kalāvatīrṇa), and who likewise is a partial portion (tadaṃśa) of it?
Who is the most perfect (paripūrṇatama), who is the complete (pūrṇa), and who is a mere fragmentary portion (kalāṃśaka)?
O Śambhu, in the propitiation of whom is there what fruit and what fame? Furthermore, what is the extensive and independent result of the distinction between the limbs and the possessor of limbs?
O Lord of Gods, what was that which was given by the sage Nārāyaṇa as a protective armor (kavaca) to the brahmin Subhadra,
and which deity is to be propitiated through it?
And this most wonderful armor,
which must be kept strictly secret and is extremely difficult to obtain in all the worlds, was not previously told to me by Brahmā.
Sanatkumāra knows it, yet he did not speak of it to me in the past; whatever auspicious knowledge you know that has not been asked of me, [please tell it].
O Lord of Blessedness, tell me that peerless essence of the Vedas which cuts away the very root of karma; show me your grace.
This unprecedented narrative of Rādhikā is extremely difficult to find even in the Vedas;
it is extremely difficult to find in the Purāṇas, the Itihāsas, and the Vedāṅgas.
And from the guru’s instruction regarding knowledge, there arises knowledge of both mantra and tantra;
that is the tantra and that is the mantra, from which devotion to Kṛṣṇa comes to be.
O Lord, some knowledge may arise for the wise from the exposition of the Vedas;
yet you are the worshipful cause of the Vedas and the presiding deity of knowledge.
Therefore, O best among the knowers of the Vedas, O Lord, please speak of that supreme knowledge to me,
who am devoted, attached, and have come to you for refuge.
Having heard the words of Nārada and of the preceptor of yogis, the Guru of gurus consulted with the Blessed Lady and prepared to speak the knowledge.
Thus has been told this entire former narrative, which is captivating,
bestows devotion to Hari, and cuts away the very root of all karma.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the *Jñānāmṛtasāra*, the first *ekarātra* of the *Śrī Nārada-pañcarātra*;
and thus concludes this *Ekarātra* of the *Nārada-pañcarātra*.
